No. 25-238 
 
 
 
CUTBERTO VIRAMONTES, et al., 
     Petitioners, 
v. 
COOK COUNTY, ILLINOIS, et al., 
    Respondents. 
 
On Writ of Certiorari to the United States Court of 
Appeals for the Seventh Circuit 
SUGGESTION OF MOOTNESS 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Eileen O’Neill Burke  
 Cook County State’s Attorney

INTRODUCTION 
On October 29, 2026, petitioners filed a motion to 
dismiss petitioner Cutberto Viramontes from this 
case. In his motion, Viramontes did not provide a basis 
for his request, nor  did he submit a declaration to 
demonstrate that the membership associations 
continue to have standing. Without Viramontes’ 
involvement, it is doubtful that any petitioner has 
Article III standing to litigate the question presented. 
Accordingly, pursuant to this Court’s Rule 21.2(b), 
Cook County respectfully suggests that if Petitioner  
Viramontes were permitted to withdraw from 
litigation, the Court should dismiss the case as moot 
or as improvidently granted.1 
ARGUMENT 
“The standing Article III requires must be met by 
persons seeking appellate review, just as it must be 
met by persons appearing in courts of first instance. ” 
Arizonans for Official English v. Arizona, 520 U.S. 43, 
64 (1997). And “[h]ere, as in all standing inquiries, the 
critical question is whether at least one petitioner has 
‘alleged such a personal stake in the outcome of the 
controversy as to warrant his invocation of federal -
court jurisdiction.’” Horne v. Flores, 557 U.S. 433, 445 
(2009) (quoting Summers v. Earth Island Institute,  
555 U.S. 488, 49 3 (2009)) (emphasis in original). 
                                                           
1 The jurisdictional issue raised would not prevent the Court from 
deciding the question presented given that Grant v. Higgins, No. 
25-566, was consolidated with this matter.

2 
Viramontes’ dismissal in this matter makes it unlikely 
that any remaining petitioner satisfies Article III’s 
criteria to litigate the question presented.  
1. Prior to his motion for dismissal from the case, 
Cutberto Viramontes had standing to press this 
appeal. In district court, Viramontes maintained that 
he was a Cook County resident who sought “ to own a 
Smith and Wesson Military & Police AR -15 style 
semiautomatic rifle .” J.A. 72; see Pet. App. 8a. 
Viramontes’ desire to own that AR -15-style weapon 
gave him a concrete stake in the question presented: 
“Whether the Second and Fourteenth Amendments 
guarantee the right to possess AR -15 platform and 
similar semiautomatic rifles.” Pet. i. But if the Court 
grants Viramontes’ motion for dismissal, he will no 
longer be a petitioner before the Court.  
2. Unlike Viramontes, petitioner Christopher 
Khaya—the other individual petitioner —does not 
appear to have standing to litigate the question 
presented in this Court.2 Khaya has not stated that he 
wishes to own an AR -15. Instead, he “wants an IMI 
[Industrial Military Industries] Galil semiautomatic 
rifle.” Pet. App. 8a (brackets in original and internal 
quotation marks omitted). In district court, petitioners 
took care to explain that the IMI Galil weapon is not  
an AR-15-style weapon: While they initially “agreed 
                                                           
2 The original plaintiffs also included Rubi Joyal, who “was 
removed in April 2022” and was not a party on appeal. Pet. App. 
7a n.1.

3 
with Defendant’s description of this weapon as” an 
“AR-15 style semiautomatic rifle,” they later 
“amended their response” to “clarif[y] that the firearm 
in question is not an AR -15 style rifle but is largely 
based on the AK-47 design.” Pet. App. 8a n.3 (internal 
quotation marks omitted); see D. Ct. Doc. 101 ¶ 6 n.1. 
While the Cook County ordinance applies to AK-
47-style weapons, the question presented in this Court 
is specifically limited to “AR -15 platform and similar 
semiautomatic rifles.” Pet. i. The Court did not grant 
review on petitioners’ broader argument that Cook 
County’s ordinance “is facially invalid under the 
Second Amendment.” Pet. App. 2a. Accordingly, 
Khaya has no “personal stake” in the question on 
which the Court granted certiorari. Horne, 557 U.S. at 
445.  
Should petitioners disavow their prior statement 
and argue that the IMI Galil weapon is “similar” to an 
AR-15, the record would not support that about -face. 
There are no record facts concerning whether the IMI 
Galil weapon operates  similarly to an AR -15. There 
are also no record facts concerning whether the IMI 
Galil weapon is “in common use for lawf ul purposes,” 
which petitioners maintain is central to the Second 
Amendment inquiry. See, e.g. , Petrs. Br. 29.  And 
public information strongly suggests that at least 
some variants of the IMI Galil weapon , which was 
manufactured in Israel,  are extremely rare in the 
United States. See, e.g., Legacy Collectibles, SOLD -

4 
Very Rare, Minty IMI Galil Model 392 , https://legacy-
collectibles.com/very-rare-minty-imi-galil-model-392 
(selling a Galil weapon and explaining that “[o]nly 
~400 of these [were] imported d uring the 1980s”).  
Thus, the record contains no facts showing that 
Khaya’s claim would  fall within the question 
presented or that he  would even prevail under 
petitioners’ own proposed Second Amendment test.  
Khaya may be an unsuitable petitioner for 
another reason, as well. Unlike Viramontes, who 
stated that he “ intend[ed] to use ” his AR -15-style 
weapon “for self- defense,” Khaya stated in district 
court that he was “most likely to use [the IMI Galil] at 
the range, to be honest.”  Pet. App. 8a. He explained 
that he would use the weapon for self -defense only if 
“the other two guns he owns—a handgun and different 
(permitted) semiautomatic rifle —are out of 
commission.” Id. at 9a (internal quotation marks 
omitted). It is therefore speculative that Khaya would 
ever use his weapon “for the core lawful purpose of 
self-defense.” District of Columbia v. Heller , 554 U.S. 
570, 630 (2008). 
To establish standing through Khaya, petitioners 
would need the Court to undertake an analysis of 
whether his IMI Galil weapon is similar to the AR-15; 
whether it is in common use; and whether petitioner 
intends to use it for self- defense. These fact -bound, 
antecedent inquiries were un necessary before 
Viramontes sought dismissal from the case. At a

5 
minimum, these difficultie s mean that the case may 
no longer be a good vehicle to answer the question on 
which the Court granted plenary review.  
3. The two petitioner membership associations —
the Firearms Policy Coalition and Second Amendment 
Foundation—also appear to lack standing  to litigate 
the question presented. See Pet. App. 7a. For a 
membership association to have standing, it must 
“make specific allegations establishing that at least 
one identified member had suffered or would suffer 
harm.” Summers, 555 U.S. at 498. I n this case, the  
organizations identified  only two members  in all of 
Cook County: Viramontes and Khaya. Pet. App. 8a; see 
D. Ct. Doc. 1, ¶¶ 12-13. For the reasons just explained, 
Khaya lacks standing to litigate the question 
presented, and so the membership associations cannot 
establish standing through him. And they equally 
cannot establish standing through Viramontes if he  
disassociates himself from the suit.  
Any suggestion from petitioners that Viramontes 
continues to want to purchase an AR -15, and so 
remains an identified member who qualifies the 
membership associations for standing , should be 
treated with skepticism . Viramontes has not offered 
any explanation as to why he sought to remove himself 
from the suit. And the most natural inference from the 
barebones motion is that Viramontes’ circumstances 
have changed in some significant fashion. Thus, if 
petitioners dispute that premise, the Court should

6 
require Viramontes to submit a declaration that he 
continues to qualify the membership associations for 
standing. Such a step would allow the Court to “assure 
that standing exists ” before deciding this case. 
Summers, 555 U.S. at 499.   
CONCLUSION  
For the foregoing reasons, this Court should 
dismiss this case as moot or improvidently granted if 
petitioner Viramontes is removed from the case. 
Respectfully submitted,
